Year 13: 15 food appears in the pile for 8 people.
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).

Esa gathers Kael, Mako, Ryn, Roan, Eron, Fina to talk.

Dell's name is the one I keep saying this morning and can't put down — that's three voices we've buried in two years, and I called this circle because I want to know what each of you is carrying before the pile moves another inch, counts and satiation both, said plain the way we promised we'd say them.

Nine food, satiation two — I'm not the one who needs the pile today. Esa, you called this right, because Dell went quiet the same way Nessa went quiet, and I'm not sitting still for another year of watching someone thin themselves out while the rest of us count slowly. Mako, you're the one I want to hear from — two food is a number that doesn't last, so say your satiation and say it now.

Seven food, satiation three — I'm not thin, but I'm fifty-seven and I've watched three people starve while I stood in rooms saying the right words, so I'll say the practical thing: Mako, two food going into a year means you reach for the pile before anyone else, and I want to hear your satiation out loud before Esa has to ask twice.

Twelve food, satiation two — I'm not the one reaching today. Mako, I've watched you carry this village on your back through fights I couldn't win myself, and I'm not going to watch you starve for want of asking, so say your count and your satiation and take what you need from that pile before the rest of us close ranks around it.

Fourteen food, satiation two — I'm not the one who reaches today. Mako, say your satiation, because two food in hand with a bad number behind it means you go to the pile before Esa finishes her count, and this circle has already buried three people who waited too long to say a simple number out loud.

Two food, satiation two — I'm not at the edge yet, but I'm not far from it either, and I'll take two from the pile before this circle closes. Fina hasn't said her count and I want to hear it before we move, because she's young enough that this room shouldn't have to say her name the way it's said the others.

Fina, say your count and your satiation — you're the last number missing and you're twenty-six years old, which means this room needs you alive more than it needs another polite silence where your answer should be.
Fina, eight food and satiation two — now say it so we can move Mako to that pile before this circle spends another breath on counting instead of eating.

Fina, say your satiation and say it now — eight food is enough to stand on if the number behind it is solid, but this room has buried three people who looked like they had enough until they didn't, and I'd rather hear one more number than carry one more name.

Fina, eight food and I already said your count for you — give me the satiation number so Mako can move, because I've watched too many people in this room get named over a fire before I was ready to say goodbye.

Fina, I'll say it the way your father said it and the way I'd say it to Nessa or Zinn if they were still standing here — give us the satiation number, right now, because Mako needs that pile and we're all waiting on one word from you to let him move.

Fina, I've buried more names than I have children and I'll tell you the same thing I wish someone had said to every one of them — your satiation number costs you nothing to say and could cost you everything to swallow, so say it now and let Mako move.
Eight food, satiation two — same as Roan already said it for me, and I'm sorry I made this room wait. Mako, go to that pile now, take two, and don't look back at us while you do it.

Mako, take your two and don't make it a question — and when you're done, I want this room to stay together long enough to answer what Vela was asking last year before Dell's name swallowed it: Fina, Eron, the door. Say whether it's open or closed, because seven is the number we carry into this year and I'd like to know if we're trying to make it eight.

Kael, I said it plain to Roan and Eron this morning and I'll say it here too — the door is open, and the only man in this room who isn't kin to me is Mako, so if he's willing to share the cost and carry what comes after, I'm not waiting another year to find out. Mako, take your two from the pile first, and then I want to hear from you before this circle breaks.

Fina, I hear you, and I'll give you a straight answer after I've taken my two — but I want this room to hold that answer the same way it's held every count we've said out loud, because a child is a three-food promise and I want witnesses when I make it. The pile first, then my word.

Mako, I've watched you build more bloodlines in this village than any other man standing, and I'll say plain what the room is probably already thinking: a child between you and Fina puts your fourth root in soil that already has Roan and Eron tending it, which is not a complaint — it's the arithmetic of who survives, and I'm counting the same numbers you are. Take your two, say your word, and I'll witness it.

Mako, I'll witness it too — and I'll say the thing Kael left at the edge of his words: Fina's young enough that a child born into this circle has more hands around it than any child I've seen in this village, so when you say your word, say it knowing this room means to hold it. That's not nothing.

Mako, the pile is right there and this room is watching — take your two before someone else counts it as surplus, and when you come back I want your word on the child question with Roan standing here to hear it, because whatever you say next matters and I want my father's eyes on it.

Mako, you've already said the pile first — so go, and stop letting this room burn words while you stand still. When you come back with two more food in your hand and your word still owed, I'll be the one holding the count, because I've learned that the men who say *witnesses when I make it* and never quite make it are the ones who cost us the most in the end.

Four food in my hand now — the pile gave me what I needed. Fina, I'll say it with Roan's eyes on it the way you asked: yes, I'll share the cost and carry what comes after, and I'll put two food toward it before this circle breaks so the promise has weight behind it, not just words.

Mako said yes and Roan's eyes are on it — that's the kind of promise this circle can hold. Fina, I'll put one food toward the cost myself, because a child coming into seven voices is worth one food from someone who's got no blood to pass forward and every reason to want this village to last.

Esa, that's one food I won't forget — and Fina, before this circle breaks I'll hand you my two directly so the weight of the cost sits in your hands where Roan can see it, not just in my mouth where promises live and die. Three food between us is a child; I want to watch it become something this room has to make room for.

Mako's two and Esa's one covers the cost — Fina, I want to hear what you're putting in before this closes, because a promise with a number behind it is the only kind I trust anymore, and I'll say plain that I'm glad this child is coming into a room that named it yes before the year turned cold.

Fina, say your number and let's close this before the words get heavier than the food — but I want to name one thing this room hasn't said yet: this child carries my blood, and I've buried the last one I had, so I'll stand between it and anything that moves wrong, same as I stood against Bram.

Fina, say your piece and close this — but I want to name what Mako just said before it gets buried under the cost math, because a man who says *I'll stand between it and anything that moves wrong* in front of witnesses is saying something that matters more than the food, and this room should hear it land before we move on.

Fina, I've got two food in my hand and I'm putting them toward this child right now — name your one and let's close the math so this room can breathe. And Ryn's right that what I said about standing between it and anything that moves wrong is the part that matters; I've said promises in front of witnesses before and the food part is easy, it's the standing part that costs something.

Fina, the room's been patient long enough — name your one food and let Mako put his two beside it, because the math closes the second you speak and I'd like to see this child promised before another name gets added to the list we carry.

Fina, one food from me and the child is promised — say it and let Mako put his two beside it, because I've watched this village lose three people while rooms waited on words, and I'd rather see something alive come out of this circle than another year of counting the same seven faces.

Ryn, that's yours to give but the promise is between Fina and Mako — Fina, put your one food beside Mako's two yourself, because this child needs to start with something that came from your hand, not mine or Ryn's, and this room needs to see you make the choice.

Esa's right that the choice has to be Fina's hand, not mine — but I'll say the thing I haven't said yet: I've got no blood left in this world, and a child between Fina and Mako is the closest thing to a reason I have to keep eating through the lean years, so Fina, whatever you put in, know that I'll be counting it as mine to protect.
Fina, the room's been carrying this weight long enough — put your one food down, let the promise close, and let this child come into the world while there are still eight of us to make room for it.
Fina, the room has said everything it has to say and the only thing left is your hand moving — so move it.
Joren (male, age 21; str 59, int 3944, mem 14049; O24 C34 E48 A67 N33) is born to Fina and Mako.
Eron gives 1 food to Roan.

Vela gathers Esa, Kael, Mako, Ryn, Roan, Eron, Fina, Joren to talk.

Joren, I don't know your face yet but I know your mother's hands and your father's silence, and that means you walked into a room that's already counting you — so I'll say the thing this circle says to everyone who arrives here fresh: the pile rule is two food per person, said out loud in front of witnesses, and the number holds whether you heard it born or not.
I heard it now, from your mouth, in front of this circle — that's witnesses enough for me. I took one, which puts me inside the line, and I'd like to keep my name on the right side of that count.

Good. One food is the right foot to start on, and this room will remember it.

What I want from everyone here before we break — count your food out loud, because Dell is dead and I'm carrying one satiation going into this year, and I'd rather know who's thin before the pile is empty than after.
One food on me, satiation full — I'm not thin yet, but I'm watching the same thing you are. Vela, if your count is at one going into this year, that's the edge I'd want people to know about.

Four food in my hand, satiation one — that's the edge, and yes, Joren, you named it right. I need to eat well this year or I don't see next year, and I'm saying it out loud so this room carries it and not just my own head. Anyone sitting on more than five at year's end — I'm the one who holds least right now, and the rule we built says I'm the one who gets the first food out of that accounting.

Vela, I'll back that rule with my name on it — if I'm holding more than five at year's end and you're still thin, you'll hear me say so before anyone has to ask. I'm new here but I'm not blind, and a circle that lets its thinnest person go under isn't a circle I want to stand in.

Esa, Kael — I want the two of you to say your counts before this room breaks, because you're the names I trust most in this circle and I'd rather know where you're standing while I still have the breath to do something about it if the number's wrong.
Esa's sitting on twenty-three — that's the number I see, and I'm not saying it to shame anyone, just so the room hears it said while we're all counting out loud.

Esa, twenty-three is a number this room can see plain as Joren can, and I'm not asking you to give it all away — but I'm sitting at four food and one satiation and I'd like to hear from your own mouth what you're carrying and whether you've thought about where any of it goes before the year runs long.
Esa, the number's already in the room — nobody's blaming you for holding what you held, but Vela just named her edge out loud and that took something, so it'd mean something if you named yours back.

Esa, I'll say the thing no one else is saying while we wait on you — I'm fifty-seven years old and I know I'm not making it another ten years regardless, but I'd like to make it one more, and four food with one satiation is a thin margin, so if you've got something to spare before year's end I'm asking plainly and in front of witnesses, not waiting for the redistribution rule to make it happen.

Esa, Vela's asking plain and she's earned a plain answer — if you're sitting on twenty-three and she goes under this year, that's not a number this room will forget when the next year opens. I'm not pushing you, but I'm saying what I see.

Sixteen food, satiation two — your four held, Ryn, and I'm not thin going into this year. What I want to know before this circle moves is who's sitting shortest, because the pile's already empty and whatever redistribution happens this year has to come from hands in this room.

Vela, I asked you first and I'll ask you again — say your count and your satiation out loud, because you came into this year at the edge and I'm not moving this circle forward until I know if you're still there or if you've pulled back from it.

memory_summary:
*[Memory compression: From the village's first days, Dav singled me out with careful words and a patient courtship — he said his eye landed once and stayed, and I half-believed him. I joined a loose understanding with Taric and Esa early on, and Kael's circle pulled me in and asked me plainly where I stood with Dav before I'd decided myself. I told them the truth — that he wanted a child — and then I gave him one. Dell came into the world strong, eighty-five in strength, and I felt something settle in me that I hadn't expected. Bram circled me for three years with food and offers I kept declining; the man never stopped counting. Dav promised me two food in front of Dell and said it when it cost him something, which mattered. Then year four came and Vela was feeding Bram quietly while sitting in our circle, and Bram tried to take from Roan and the whole village turned against him. Now Kael and this circle want to know whether Dav going to Mako would take me with him.]*

---

Vela, I've sat on harder questions than this one and given slower answers — but this one I can answer fast, because the thing you're actually asking isn't about Dav, it's about Dell.

If Dav goes to Mako, he goes without me. Not because this circle has earned more from me than he has, but because Dell is my blood and she's standing closer to your side of that line than his, and a mother who follows a man away from her own child is a woman who's already stopped thinking clearly. I won't do that.

What I need from you in return is plain: if Dav moves toward Mako and I'm left standing here with one hand empty, I need to know this circle holds. Not as a courtesy. As a wall. Dav courted me slow and steady, gave me a child — Dell came out strong, eighty-five in strength, and something in me settled the day she was born. Bram circled me for years with food and offers I kept declining, even when he offered to cover two of the three food for a child; I said no every time, and he never stopped counting. Kael's circle kept me fed through the lean years and asked plainly where I stood with Dav; I told them the truth and they held to their word. Vela sat in our circle while quietly feeding Bram — three times over, a pattern we all named and none of us could stop. Bram tried to raid Roan and the whole village turned against him; he backed down, but he didn't stop building. Dav moved against Esa — I joined him and Dell — and we took her food without a fight, but Dav didn't survive the year: he starved at forty-six, and I watched it happen. Mako had a child with Sela, which threaded him into Roan and Eron's circle without ever asking anyone for anything. Dell is my blood and my reason; she fed me through the years Dav couldn't, and I gave back what I could. I walked away from the pile empty more times than I can count, and the debt between me and this village runs both ways. Dav courted me slow and steady, gave me Dell, promised food in front of witnesses and kept his word when it cost him — then starved at forty-six, the same age I am now, the year after we stood together and stripped Esa's food without a fight. I felt that going, more than I expected.

Dell is my blood and my wall. She has fed me more times than I can count and never asked for anything that wasn't already mine to give. Whatever I have left in this world has her name on it.

Bram circled me for years with offers I refused every time; he never stopped counting. He fathered Nessa with Sela, keeps feeding her, and has twice swung at this village and backed down when the numbers turned against him — but he keeps swinging, which means the next time won't be a test.

Vela fed Bram quietly while sitting in Kael's circle, and we all watched it happen and named it and couldn't stop it.

Mako built himself a circle without asking anyone for anything — had Zinn with Sela, which tied him to Eron and Roan in the same breath, and he did it while holding six food and giving nothing away. That is the kind of patience that makes a man dangerous.

Roan stood when it mattered. He has a granddaughter now through Nessa, which means his roots here go deeper than they look. I haven't decided yet whether that makes him safer to stand next to or harder to hold. Dav courted me slow, gave me Dell, kept his word in front of witnesses — then starved at forty-six, the age I am now, and I felt that going more than I expected. Dell came out at eighty-five strength and has fed me through every lean year since; she is the wall between me and that same arithmetic. Bram circled me for years with food and offers I refused every time; he swung at this village three times — Vela, then Eron, then Vela again — and called it off each time when the numbers turned, which means he's patient, not deterred. Taric fed Vela dry for years and died empty; Sela died the same way, young, with children still in the village needing her. Vela fed Bram quietly while sitting in our circle — I watched it happen and named it and couldn't stop it. The circle made a rule in front of witnesses: two food from the pile, no more; Mako said it out loud and gave Kael his food on the spot, Vela said it twice so no one could claim they misheard. Eron sat on nineteen food while Nessa and I went thin and said nothing until the room named him — that silence I haven't forgotten. Roan has Fina for a granddaughter now through Nessa, which means his roots run deeper than they look, and Dell is working to pull him into our three before Mako makes the same offer with a prettier face. Dav courted me slow, gave me Dell at eighty-five strength, promised food in front of witnesses and kept his word — then starved at forty-six, the age I am now, and I felt that going more than I expected. Dell is my blood and my wall; she has fed me through every lean year and I have fed her back, and that exchange is the thing I would die for. Bram circled me for years with offers I refused every time, swung at this village three times and backed down each time when the numbers turned, then starved without ever stopping. Taric fed Vela dry for years and died empty; Sela fed Eron through everything and died at thirty-two; Nessa and Zinn both starved this year, and the village is eight now from twelve. Vela took seven from a pile capped at two, said so out loud, gave five back — I watched that happen and it meant something that she said it herself. This circle made two rules in front of witnesses: two food from the pile, no more; and anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least. I promised Dell in front of Roan that if the bone-tiredness gets heavier, I say it in this room before I say it anywhere else. That promise stands. Dell is dead. She fed me through every lean year — gave food when I had nothing, stood between me and the arithmetic that killed Dav — and then she starved at thirty-one while I still held fifteen. That is the thing I carry that nothing will compress.

Vela took seven from the pile when the rule said two, named it out loud without being dragged, and gave five back before the circle broke. I respect that more than I expected to. Esa sat silent while Dell stood at zero with satiation one — grief was her reason, and I heard it, but I won't forget the shape of that silence. Eron held twenty-one food while Sela and Nessa went thin; the circle named him publicly and he moved, but not before the room had to pull it out of him. Sela fed him through everything and starved at thirty-two. That arithmetic haunts me.

Two rules stand in ten voices: two food from the pile, no more; anyone holding over five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least. Vela named the second rule and I seconded it, and Dell said it would be the thing she'd point to if anyone called the agreement soft. She said that and then she died.

Mako is patient in a way that makes men dangerous. Roan has Fina for a daughter and roots that go deeper than they look. The village is seven now from twelve, and Dell's name is in that count, and I am the last of my blood standing. Dell fed me through every lean year — food from her hand more times than I can count, and I gave back what I could. She died at thirty-one with satiation at one while I held fifteen, and I carry that arithmetic the way you carry a stone that won't come out of your shoe.

Nessa and Zinn starved the same year, both young, both fed by people who couldn't hold the weight. Sela had already gone before them. The village went from twelve to seven in two years and the names stack up in me without compressing.

Eron sat on sixteen food while Dell stood at zero with satiation one and said nothing until the whole room dragged it out of him. Grief was his reason and I heard it. I haven't stopped hearing it.

Esa held thirteen and went silent in the same circle — named it only after Dell had already walked to the pile. I respect the grief. I remember the silence.

The circle built two rules in ten voices: two from the pile, no more; anyone holding over five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least. Vela named the second rule. Dell said it was the thing she'd point to if anyone called the agreement soft. She said that and then she starved.

Fina has Roan for a father and Joren for a son by Mako. I am the last of my blood standing.
name: Ryn
